title: I replaced one rule with an AI "risk agent." It made my strategy worse.
author: Cautious-Rabbit-44
selftext:
I've been experimenting with an AI portfolio manager on paper for the past couple of weeks.

One thing I kept coming back to was risk.

Most strategies I see are pretty good at finding entries. Very few spend much time deciding when not to buy something.  
So I tried adding a simple "risk agent."

The base strategy is boring.

Rank a universe of large-cap tech stocks by 3-month momentum.  
Buy the top five.  
Rebalance monthly.

Then I added another step.

Before a stock could make it into the portfolio, the agent had to argue against the trade.

It looked at things like:  
Trend  
Recent drawdown  
Volatility

Whether the original thesis still made sense  
I was expecting fewer drawdowns.

Instead I mostly got... fewer winners.

The funny part is that the names the risk layer rejected often turned out to be the strongest performers a month later.  
Looking back, I think I made a common mistake.

I treated "looks risky" as the same thing as "is a bad investment."  
Those aren't the same thing.

High-beta winners usually look uncomfortable while they're working.  
So now I'm scrapping the pass/fail logic completely.

Instead of saying:  
Don't buy this.

I'm testing:  
Buy less until confidence improves.

That feels closer to how an actual portfolio manager would think.

One thing I've learned building this is that generating trade ideas is surprisingly easy.  
Building a good risk engine is much harder.

That's turning into the interesting problem.

comments.author: AttitudeGrouchy33
comments.body:
This is a good failure mode to post because “risk agent” sounds obviously smart until it quietly becomes a second noisy model.

I would probably stop treating it as a veto layer for a bit and grade it as its own worker:

- how often did it block winners vs losers
- did it add information the base strategy did not already price in
- did it behave consistently across regimes
- did it overreact to volatility that was already part of the edge
- could a dumb rule have done the same job cheaper

A lot of AI trading systems get worse when the model is asked to be a vague adult in the room. The mandate has to be narrow. “Find unknown risk in this exact setup” is different from “tell me if this feels risky.”

This is also why I like the hire/fire framing for agents. If the risk agent makes the system worse, it should lose scope or get fired, not get more prompts. We are building milo around that idea for trading agents: visible diary, bounded mandate, performance you can judge. https://app.andmilo.com/?code=@milo4reddit
